prompt: Why should a pipeline build the artefact once and promote it, rather than rebuilding for each environment?
answer_markdown: Because rebuilding from the same commit can produce different bytes. Between your staging build and your prod build, a base image tag may have been repointed, a transitive dependency may have published a patch, or the build environment may differ in some way — each individually unlikely and collectively routine. The result is that production runs a binary no test ever executed, which is the specific mechanism behind a large share of "but it passed in staging" incidents. Building once and promoting an immutable digest makes "what we tested" and "what we deployed" identical by construction rather than by hope, and it means the deployment record actually identifies the bytes that ran. There is also a valuable corollary: if an image must be rebuilt to change environments, it is environment-specific, so build-once forces configuration out of the image and into runtime injection, which is a design improvement in its own right.

prompt: How do you decide the order of pipeline stages?
answer_markdown: By cost, not by importance. Cheap fast checks first — format, lint, typecheck, unit tests — then a gate, then expensive ones like integration tests, end-to-end suites, image builds and scans. The reason is that time-to-a-red-signal determines whether the pipeline actually changes behaviour: if a missing semicolon takes eighteen minutes to report because the e2e suite runs first, developers context-switch, batch their pushes and stop watching, so the pipeline still catches bugs but no longer influences anyone. There is no value in compiling code that fails a linter. Within the cheap tier, run everything in parallel since none of those checks needs another's output, which makes the tier cost its slowest member rather than the sum. A refinement worth mentioning: within a tier, put the check most likely to fail earliest.

prompt: Why use OIDC federation instead of storing cloud access keys in your CI system?
answer_markdown: A long-lived static key has a bad shape in three ways: it never expires, it works from anywhere, and it is readable by anyone who can edit a workflow file — so a leak is a valid credential until somebody notices and rotates it. OIDC replaces the stored secret with an exchange. The CI system issues a short-lived signed token describing the run — which repository, which branch, which workflow — and the cloud provider is configured to trust that issuer and swap such a token for temporary credentials, but only when the claims match a policy you wrote. Three properties improve at once: credentials expire in minutes so a leak has a tiny window, they are scoped by claim so a role can be restricted to one branch in one repository and a pull-request branch cannot assume the production role, and there is nothing stored to rotate or exfiltrate because there is no stored secret.

prompt: Several security tools run as sequential steps in one CI job with a single overall timeout. The last tool is reported as timing out. You give it more CPU and nothing changes. What is actually happening?
answer_markdown: The last tool almost certainly never ran. An earlier slow step consumed the shared time budget, so the later step was starved of the clock, and the failure gets reported as that later tool timing out — pointing blame at entirely the wrong component. The diagnostic tell is specific: the accused step shows no evidence of having done any work at all. No CPU time consumed, no CPU throttling recorded, no process ever present, no output beyond a start line, no partial results. A tool that is genuinely too slow leaves traces of working; one that was never scheduled leaves none. There is a second mechanism layered on top that makes this worse: some CI systems ignore per-step resource limits and apply a single allocation to the whole job, so raising the limit on the blamed step changes nothing because it was never applied. Two mechanisms both pointing away from the real cause is why this specific failure burns so many hours. The general lesson is to verify the blamed component actually executed before tuning it — zero work done is not a performance problem, and structurally, tools that need their own clock should get their own job.

prompt: Your remote build cache appears to be configured and the pipeline is green, but builds are not getting faster. How do you verify whether the cache is actually working?
answer_markdown: Do not trust the status endpoint. Some cache status endpoints return success for any token, valid or not, so hitting one and seeing a 200 confirms only that the endpoint is reachable — it is not evidence the cache is usable. A misconfigured team, scope or token can leave every build a cache miss while the pipeline stays entirely green, so you are paying for a cache and getting nothing with no log line saying so. Instead, probe a real artefact whose identity you know: a 404 for something that should not exist and a 200 for something that should are both genuine signals. Then confirm from build timings that hits are actually occurring, because a cache doing its job changes duration and that is the only proof that matters. A wrong scope also carries the opposite risk of serving artefacts built from different inputs. The pattern generalises: a green status is not evidence that work happened, so verify the effect rather than the report.

prompt: What belongs in the image at build time versus injected at runtime, and how do you test the boundary?
answer_markdown: Build time carries only what is genuinely universal across every environment: source code, dependencies, compiled output. Anything environment-specific — database URLs, log levels, feature flags, API endpoints, credentials — is a runtime input supplied by environment variables, mounted config or a config service. The test to apply to any image is whether that exact image could run in production and in dev, differing only in what is injected at start-up. If the answer is no, something environment-specific is baked in and needs lifting out. This matters because it is the precondition for building once and promoting: if the image has to be rebuilt to move between environments, then per-environment rebuilds are unavoidable and you lose the guarantee that production runs the bytes you tested.
